check:0:0.q: Why not “Rewriting adds 1 point, so keep it”?
check:0:0.a:
**Why "Rewriting adds 1 point, so keep it" falls short**

It gets one thing right. The score did drop from 86% to 85%, so on paper rewriting "adds 1 point."

What it misses is how small that is. On 100 questions, 1 point is just one question. That could easily be **noise**, meaning random wobble in the results. A model might answer one borderline question differently on a second run, with or without rewriting.

The paired check from "Comparing on the same examples" shows why. You count only the questions where the two versions disagree. The gap, multiplied by itself, must be at least 4 times the number of disagreements. A gap of 1 gives 1 times 1, which is 1. Even with just one disagreement, it needs 4. So a 1-question gap never passes.

The answer also skips the cost. Rewriting is an extra step to run, pay for and debug. Keeping it needs real evidence, not a one-question difference.

**Why "Its effect is within the noise" is better:** it reads the 1-point drop as too small to tell apart from chance, so rewriting becomes a candidate to remove.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Rewriting hurts, so drop it now”?
check:0:2.a:
"Rewriting hurts" claims more than the numbers show.

**What it gets right:** a part with no measurable effect is a fair candidate to remove. Less to run, pay for and debug.

**What it misses:** two things.

1. **The direction is backwards.** The 1-point dip came when rewriting was *removed*, from 86% to 85%. So the score didn't fall when rewriting was there. Still, that dip is far too small to show anything, in either direction.
2. **It skips the check.** On 100 questions, 1 point is a 1-question gap. The paired check compares the two versions on the same questions. It counts only the questions where they disagree. A 1-question gap never passes that check. You can't tell a real effect from luck, which is what "noise" means here.

So the honest finding is "we can't tell." Rewriting becomes a candidate to delete because it showed no measurable value. It is not proven harmful.

**Why "Its effect is within the noise" is the right option:** it says exactly what the data supports, that the gap is too small to show help or harm.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Remove it: one answer got better”?
check:1:1.a:
"Remove it: one answer got better" looks at only one side of the result. It does get one thing right: that 1 answer really did improve without the reranker. So the reranker is not perfect. Sometimes its reordering pushes a good search result down.

But it ignores the other side. Without the reranker, 20 answers that used to pass now fail. That is 20 losses against 1 win. The net effect is 19 fewer passing answers out of 200. That is a big drop, not an improvement.

The paired check makes this concrete. "Paired" means you compare the same questions under both versions and count only the ones where they disagree. Here 21 questions disagree, and the gap is 19. The lesson's rule asks whether the gap times itself is at least 4 times the number of disagreements. 19 times 19 is 361. 4 times 21 is 84. So 361 clears 84 easily. The drop is real, not noise.

Judging a part by one lucky question is how useful parts get deleted by mistake.

"Keep the reranker: it does real work" is better because it weighs all 21 changed answers, and they show the reranker clearly earns its place.

judge.notes: Minor: the claim that the reranker 'pushes a good result down' is the tutor's own guess, not from the lesson, and at about 196 words the answer is close to the length limit.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Nothing yet: it could just be luck”?
check:1:2.a:
"It could just be luck" has a sensible instinct behind it. Scores do wobble from run to run, and a small drop can be noise. Being careful before you act is a good habit.

But here you don't have to guess. You can check. The lesson's paired check looks only at the questions where the two versions disagree:

- Only the full pipeline passed: 20 questions
- Only the version without the reranker passed: 1 question

That is 21 disagreements, and the gap between the two counts is 19. Use the rule from the lesson. 19 times 19 is 361. Four times 21 is 84. Since 361 is far more than 84, the drop is real.

If luck were behind it, the flips would split roughly evenly in both directions. Twenty against one is not an even split. So "Nothing yet" ignores evidence you already have and treats a clear result as unclear.

"Keep the reranker: it does real work" is better because the paired check shows that removing it consistently breaks answers, far beyond what chance would explain.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The arithmetic matches the lesson's rule (19² = 361 against 4 × 21 = 84), though it never states the rule outright, and the answer is close to the 200-word limit.

check:2:0.q: Why not “The reranker was worth 5 points”?
check:2:0.a:
That answer gets one thing right. Something you took out mattered, because the score fell by 5 points.

But it gives all the credit to the reranker, and the run can't support that. You removed two parts at once: the reranker and query rewriting. The 5-point drop belongs to the pair, not to either one alone.

Several stories fit the same number:

- The reranker did all of it, and rewriting did nothing.
- Rewriting did all of it, and the reranker did nothing.
- Each did some.
- The two parts depend on each other. For example, the reranker might only help when the search query has been rewritten first.

One run can't tell these apart. That is why an ablation removes **one part at a time** and keeps everything else the same. Then any drop has only one possible cause.

To learn the reranker's real contribution, rerun with only the reranker switched off. Then check the drop with the paired check: count only the questions where the two versions disagree.

"You can't tell which part did it" is better because it claims only what the run shows: two parts changed together, so the drop can't be split between them.

judge.notes: Minor: 'Something you took out mattered' treats the 5-point drop as real without the paired check the lesson requires, but this does not contradict the lesson.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Query rewriting was worth 5 points”?
check:2:1.a:
That answer gets one thing right. Something you removed mattered, because the score fell 5 points. So the two parts *together* were worth about 5 points.

What it misses is that you changed two things at once. The drop belongs to the pair, not to query rewriting alone. The 5 points could all come from the reranker. They could all come from the rewrite. They could be split between them in any mix.

The parts can also interact, which means they affect each other. For example, the rewrite might only help when the reranker is there to sort what it finds. Then neither part has a clean "worth" when you pull both out together.

The lesson's own example shows the risk. Removed one at a time, the rewrite cost 1 point and the reranker cost 7. A joint run would hide that difference completely.

That is why an ablation removes **one** part per run and keeps everything else the same.

"You can't tell which part did it" is better because it states exactly what the evidence supports: a 5-point drop for the pair, with no way to divide it between them.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Measure the drop, then sort” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

**The problem:** "Pipelines pile up parts over time, like query rewriting, a reranker or memory. Each one costs money, time and debugging. But nobody knows which ones actually help."

**The idea:** "So I run an ablation. That means I switch off one part, keep everything else the same, and rerun the same eval questions. The score drop is that part's contribution. I do this for each part, then sort by drop, biggest first. The top is what I'd miss most. A part with no drop is a candidate to delete."

**The trade-off:** "Small drops can just be noise. A 1-point drop on 100 questions is one question. So I use a paired check. I only count the questions where the two versions disagree, before calling a drop real."

**A likely follow-up**

*"What if two parts do the same job?"*

Hint at a strong answer: each one alone might show zero drop, because the other covers for it. Then you'd wrongly delete both. Say you'd also remove them together to catch this overlap, then keep the cheaper one.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Signs ablations were skipped or done wrong**

- **Parts nobody can justify.** Each run gets slower and costs more, but the score barely moves. Nobody can say what the reranker or memory adds.
- **Two things changed at once.** An ablation removed two parts, or used a different question set. Then you can't tell which change caused the drop.
- **Small gaps treated as real.** A 1 or 2 point drop is called "this part matters." On 100 questions that's one or two questions, which is noise (random wobble between runs).
- **Small rises treated as real, too.** A score that goes up slightly when a part is removed is just as likely to be noise. It needs the same paired check before you conclude anything.
- **The "off" part still runs.** A trace (the record of every step a run took, which MLflow can show you) still lists the `rerank` step in the run without it. The switch didn't work, so that ablation's number is meaningless.

**Quickest check**

Open one trace from each ablation run. Confirm the removed step is truly absent. Confirm every run used the same questions. Then, for any gap you plan to act on, count only the questions where the two versions disagree and apply the paired check.

judge.notes: It runs to about 210 words, over the 200-word limit, and it uses "paired check" without explaining it, which a beginner may not follow. It also brings in MLflow, which this lesson never mentions.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Parts that cover for each other.** Removing the query rewrite alone might show no drop, because the reranker quietly fixes the same mistakes. Remove both and the score could fall a lot. When two parts do similar jobs, also try removing them together before you delete either one.

**2. Questions that never use the part.** Memory scored 0 points, but if every eval question is a single, fresh question, memory never got a chance to help. A 0 here means "untested," not "useless." Add follow-up questions that rely on earlier turns, then rerun the ablation.

**3. Too few questions, or a jumpy LLM.** With 30 questions, even a useful part may never pass the paired check. An LLM can also answer differently on each run, which blurs small drops. Collect more questions, or run each version a few times and compare the averages before deciding.

In each case, a small or zero drop is a reason to look closer, not proof the part does nothing.

learn:term.a:
**Design** and **Evaluate** are two stages of the same job. Design is planning. Evaluate is reading the results.

In Design, you decide what to test before running anything. For ablations, you list extra versions of your best pipeline, each with one part switched off. In the lesson's code, that means calling `build_graph(use_rerank=False)` or `build_graph(use_rewrite=False)`.

In Evaluate, you run every version on the same 100 questions and judge the drops. You use the **paired check**: look only at the questions where the two versions disagree, one passing and the other failing. A small gap there is **noise**, meaning random wobble, not a real effect.

Think of cooking. Design is deciding to make the soup once without salt and once without garlic. Evaluate is tasting each one against the original.

In the example, Design planned three versions. Evaluate looked at the **reranker**, a model that reorders search results so the best come first. On 8 questions, only the full pipeline passed. On 1, only the version without it passed. That gap of 7 is real. Removing memory changed nothing.

judge.notes: It uses 'ablations' and 'pipeline' without explaining them, drops in code calls like build_graph(use_rerank=False), runs to about 200 words, and 'Design planned three versions' is loose because there are three ablation variants plus the full pipeline.

check:0:0.q: Why not “More setups, to find a cheaper one”?
check:0:0.a:
"More setups" isn't crazy. A cheaper setup that still scores well might exist, and trying more options is a normal next step.

But the question asks what the experiment should have had **from the start**. More setups is something you do *after* you hit the problem. It doesn't fix the cause.

The cause is that nothing said "cost matters" before the runs began. So the 12 setups were judged on quality alone, and the winner ended up costing three times what you can spend. If you add 12 more setups without changing that, you can land in the same spot again. You'd spend more time and money and still have no clear way to choose.

A **decision rule** is the sentence you write before any run, like "highest quality at $2 or less per 1,000 requests." It tells you which runs count and which to skip. It also shapes which setups are worth trying at all.

"A decision rule that includes the budget" is better because it builds the cost limit into the plan from day one, so the experiment ends in a choice you can actually afford.

check:0:2.q: Why not “A bigger model, to lift quality”?
check:0:2.a:
"A bigger model" sounds sensible, because bigger models often do score higher on quality. That part is fair.

But it answers a different question. The Check asks what the experiment should have had **from the start**. A bigger model is just one more setup to try. It is not part of the plan for judging the setups you already have.

It also makes the real problem worse. Your best setup already costs three times your budget. A bigger model usually costs *more* per request, so it would likely land even further over the limit.

The real gap is that nobody said what "best" meant before running anything. Twelve setups were scored, but the winner was picked on quality alone, so it ignored cost. That is how you end up with a top result you can't afford to ship.

**A decision rule that includes the budget** is better because, written down in Design, it would have pointed straight to the highest-quality setup that fits the budget, so the experiment ends in a decision you can act on.

judge.notes: No major problem. The claims that bigger models usually score higher and cost more come from outside the lesson, though they are reasonable and do not contradict it.

check:1:1.q: Why not “A second new prompt to compare it with”?
check:1:1.a:
It's a fair instinct. A score of 82% on its own means nothing, so you do need something to compare it with. That part is right.

The problem is *what* you compare it with. The question asks whether the new prompt **helped**. "Helped" means "made things better than before." A second new prompt is not "before." It's just another untested idea.

Say the second prompt scores 78%. Now you know the first new prompt beats the second one. But you still don't know if either beats what you already have. Your current prompt might score 85%. Then both new prompts made things worse, and you'd never see it.

That's why you need a **baseline**: the version you have now, run the same way. "The same way" matters too. Use the same eval set (your fixed list of test questions), the same model and the same judge. Then the prompt is the only thing that changed. So any gap in the score is down to the prompt.

**Why the other answer wins:** "The current version's score, run the same way" is better because it answers the real question, "is this better than what we have?", with only one thing changed.

check:1:2.q: Why not “A bigger model to run it on”?
check:1:2.a:
A bigger model doesn't answer the question. The question is whether the new prompt helped. To know that, you need something to compare the 82% against.

Is there anything right about it? A bigger model might well push the score up. But that is the problem. It adds a second change on top of the prompt. The model is meant to be a **control**: something you hold fixed so it can't affect the result. Swap it, and if the score moves, you can't tell whether the prompt or the model did it. The test is no longer fair.

It also leaves the real gap open. Even with a bigger model, 82% still has nothing to be better than. Maybe the old prompt scored 85%. Maybe it scored 70%. You can't know.

"The current version's score, run the same way" is better because it gives you a **baseline**. That is the score of what you have now, on the same eval set, model and judge. Then the prompt is the only difference, and any change in score can be put down to it.

judge.notes: No real problems. The closing explanation runs to three sentences although the prompt asked for one, and 'eval set' and 'judge' are used without explanation, but these are minor.

The difference is about *who decides the value*.

- A **metric** is something you measure after the run. The run produces it.

You did not pick 0.81. It came out of scoring the app on the eval set, probably with an LLM judge grading each answer. It is the *result* of the experiment, not one of its inputs.

check:2:2.a:
The eval results file does belong in the run. Saving it is a good habit, because it keeps the evidence behind your score. But it is an **artifact**, not a parameter.

The difference is about direction:

- A **parameter** is something you *set* before the run. It is an input you chose on purpose.
- A **metric** is a number you *measured*, like quality at 0.81.
- An **artifact** is a *file* the run produces or keeps, like the eval results.

```python
mlflow.log_artifact("eval_results.json")  # artifact: a file you keep
```

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Skip over budget, keep the best” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer:**

**The problem.** "I'd run several versions of an app, say different chunk sizes. Each one gets a quality score and a cost. Without a rule decided in advance, it's tempting to pick whichever looks best afterwards. That isn't a fair decision."

**The idea.** "So I write the rule down first: highest quality at $2 or less per 1,000 requests. I treat the budget as a hard filter, so anything over it is out. Among the runs that fit, the highest quality wins. It's like buying the best phone you can afford."

**The trade-off.** "A hard limit is simple and honest, but it's blunt. A run that's slightly over budget with much better quality still gets dropped. If that matters, I'd change the rule before the next experiment, not after seeing the results."

**A likely follow-up:** *"Why not pick the highest quality first, then check the cost?"*

**Hint for a strong answer:** The budget is part of the decision rule, not an afterthought. Filtering first means an over-budget run can never win, even by accident. Mention that MLflow's `search_runs` supports this directly: a `filter_string` for the budget, then `order_by` for quality.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **A big jump you can't explain.** Two runs differ in several parameters, like `chunk_size` and `model`. The score rose, but you can't say which change caused it.
- **No baseline in the folder.** Your new run scores 0.81, but nothing in the MLflow experiment shows the current version run the same way. A number alone tells you nothing.
- **Scores drift between identical setups.** The eval set or the LLM judge (the grading model) changed quietly between runs. A control slipped, so the comparison isn't fair.
- **Great in testing, worse in real use.** The eval set was tweaked until the new version won. It no longer reflects real questions.
- **The "winner" keeps changing.** If people argue over which run is best, the decision rule was probably picked after seeing the results.

**Quickest check**

Open the MLflow experiment and compare the runs side by side in the UI. Look at the parameters column. Exactly one parameter should differ from the baseline run. The eval set and judge should match. Then find where the decision rule was written down, and confirm it was written before the runs.

learn:stops.a:
**1. A small eval set or a noisy judge.** With only 20 questions, a score of 0.81 against 0.80 may just be luck. An LLM judge can also grade the same answer differently on different runs. Use a bigger eval set, run each version more than once, and treat tiny gaps as ties.

**2. Data that changes over time.** Real user questions drift (slowly shift) away from your eval set. A baseline scored months ago on old questions is no longer a fair comparison. Refresh the eval set with real questions from monitoring, then re-score the baseline on that same set.

**3. Settings that affect each other.** Chunk size and `k` (how many chunks you fetch) often interact. The best chunk size at `k` = 5 may not be best at `k` = 10. Changing one thing at a time can miss the best mix. So plan a small grid (every combination of a few values) in Design, and log every parameter.

In each case the core idea holds. Keep the comparison fair, and write the decision rule down first.

learn:term.a:
A **run** is the whole record of one attempt. **Parameters** are one part inside that record: the settings you chose for that attempt.

Think of a baking notebook. A run is one page, for one cake. The parameters are the settings you wrote on that page, like oven temperature and baking time. The same page also holds what you measured (**metrics**, like a taste score) and files you kept (**artifacts**, like a photo).

In the lesson's example, `mlflow.start_run(run_name="cs512-k5")` opens one run. Inside it, `mlflow.log_params` records the parameters: `chunk_size` 512, `k` 5 and `model` `"fast-model"`. Then `mlflow.log_metrics` records `quality` 0.81 and `cost_per_1k` 1.8 on that same run.

The two work together. Each run keeps its parameters right next to its metrics. So when you compare runs in one experiment, you can see which settings went with which scores. Say two runs differ in only one parameter, and the controls (eval set, model, prompt) stayed fixed. Then a difference in score can be put down to that one parameter.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Retrieval: it is the first step”?
check:0:0.a:
"Retrieval: it is the first step" sounds sensible. Retrieval often is the weak link in a RAG app, and checking it early is a fair instinct. But being first in the chain doesn't make a step the problem. The oracle test (swapping one step for a perfect version) has already checked retrieval for you.

Look at the numbers. The app scores 70%. When you hand the model the right documents directly, it scores 72%. So retrieval's **headroom**, the most you could ever gain by making it perfect, is just 2 points. Even flawless retrieval leaves the app failing 28% of the time.

That means most of the failures happen *after* the documents arrive. The model has the right information and still gets the answer wrong. Spending weeks tuning retrieval would chase 2 points at most.

"Generation: the prompt or the model" is better because the oracle run shows the right documents barely help, so the remaining errors must come from how the model turns those documents into an answer.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The claim that retrieval 'often is the weak link' goes beyond the lesson, but it is hedged and doesn't contradict it.

check:0:2.a:
"Nowhere" gets one thing right. Retrieval is not worth more work. Perfect documents only lift you from 70% to 72%. That is just 2 points of **headroom**, meaning the most you could ever gain by perfecting that step.

But it misses the bigger picture. Even with the right documents handed over directly, the app still gets 28% of questions wrong. Those failures can't be blamed on retrieval, because retrieval was perfect in that run. So they must come from a later step: the part that reads the documents and writes the answer. That part is called **generation**.

Also, "good enough" is a business decision, not something the oracle test tells you. The test's job is to point at where the errors live. Here it points clearly away from retrieval and toward what comes after it. Whether 70% is acceptable depends on your users and goals, which the question never mentions.

"Generation: the prompt or the model" is better because the oracle run shows that most of the remaining errors happen after the right documents arrive, so that is where the real headroom is.

judge.notes: No real problems; the 'business decision' remark goes slightly beyond the lesson, and the claim that the remaining errors must come from generation is a reasonable inference rather than something the lesson states.

check:1:1.q: Why not “A grid of every chunk size and k”?
check:1:1.a:
A grid search means trying every combination of settings and scoring each one. Here the settings are **chunk size** (how big each piece of a document is when you split it up) and **k** (how many pieces retrieval hands back per question).

What it gets right: it is a real way to tune retrieval. It might find a better setting.

What it misses: the grid *is* the month of tuning, or a big chunk of it. It costs many eval runs. And it only tells you the best of the settings you happened to try. It can't tell you how much better retrieval could ever get. So it can't answer the actual question: is retrieval worth the effort at all?

If perfect documents only lift you from 78% to 80%, every cell in that grid was wasted work. The problem lives in another step.

The oracle run costs one eval. It shows the ceiling, the most that fixing retrieval could ever gain you, before you spend anything on tuning it.

That is why "A run that hands it the right documents" is better: one cheap run tells you whether the month of tuning has any real headroom to win.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The same eval again, to check the score”?
check:1:2.a:
Rerunning the same eval isn't wrong. It just answers a different question.

**What it gets right:** it confirms your current score, say 78%. That number is your **baseline**, the starting point you compare against. Running it twice can also show how much the score wobbles from run to run.

**What it misses:** it only tells you where you are, not where you could get. The system hasn't changed, so the score won't tell you anything about retrieval. A bad answer could come from retrieval, reranking, or the prompt. Another identical run can't separate those. You'd still be guessing before committing a month of work.

The question you actually need answered is "If retrieval were perfect, how much better would we do?" That gap is retrieval's **headroom**: the most you could gain by fixing that one step. If it's 2 points, the month is wasted. If it's 13 points, it's well spent.

**Why "A run that hands it the right documents" is better:** it swaps retrieval for a perfect version, so the score jump shows exactly how much tuning retrieval could ever win you.

check:2:0.a:
More questions is a fair instinct. A bigger eval set (the list of test questions you score against) makes your scores steadier. With only a few questions, one lucky or unlucky answer can swing the result. So more questions help you trust that a gap like 78% versus 80% is real and not just noise.

But size isn't what an oracle test needs. The oracle replaces retrieval with a perfect version. To do that, it has to know what "perfect" looks like for each question. That means knowing which documents are the right ones.

Look at the lesson's `oracle_app`. It takes `gold_doc_ids`, the correct document ids for each question, and fetches those directly with `lookup`. If your eval set has no such ids, there is nothing to hand the model. Doubling the questions just gives you twice as many questions with no right documents attached. The oracle still can't run.

"The right document for each question" is better because it is the one thing the oracle can't work without: it supplies the perfect input that the oracle swaps in for retrieval.

check:2:1.a:
A bigger model sounds helpful, but it doesn't give you what an oracle retrieval test needs.

**What it gets partly right:** a stronger model can improve answers. Some teams also use one as a "judge" (a model that grades answers). But neither of those is an oracle for retrieval.

**What it misses:** an oracle retrieval test swaps the retrieval step for a *perfect* version. That means handing the model the exact right documents for each question. A bigger model doesn't know which documents are right. If you asked it to pick them, it would just be another guess, not a perfect answer. So you couldn't trust the gap you measured.

Swapping in a bigger model also changes the *generation* step (writing the answer), not retrieval. You would be testing the wrong part of the chain.

In the lesson's code, `oracle_app` takes `gold_doc_ids`. "Gold" means the known-correct labels. Those have to be written into your eval set ahead of time.

**Why "The right document for each question" is better:** without those known-correct document ids, there is no perfect retrieval to swap in, so there is nothing to compare against.

judge.notes: No real problems; the mention of a model 'judge' isn't in the lesson, but it doesn't contradict it.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Find the step with most headroom” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem:* "A RAG app first looks up documents, then answers from them. That makes it a chain of steps. When an answer is wrong, any step could be to blame. So teams often tune the wrong one."

*The idea:* "I run an oracle test. I swap one step for a perfect version, like handing the model the right documents. Then I rerun the eval, which is my scored set of test questions. The gain over my current score is that step's headroom: the most I could win by fixing it. I work on the step with the biggest headroom first."

*The trade-off:* "Oracles need the right answer for each step, like the correct document ids for every question. Labeling that takes work. Also, headroom is a ceiling, not a promise. Real fixes usually land below it."

**A likely follow-up:** "What if two oracles each show only small gains?"

*Hint for a strong answer:* Steps can depend on each other. Better reranking (reordering found documents so the best come first) can't help if retrieval never found the right document. Run an oracle on both steps together to see their combined headroom.

judge.notes: No real problems. The follow-up hint (running an oracle on two steps together) goes slightly beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Signs the idea was skipped:** you spend days tuning one step, like retrieval, and the eval score barely moves. That usually means the real problem sits in a different step, and nobody measured headroom first. (Headroom is the most you could gain by making that step perfect.)

**Signs the oracle run itself went wrong:**

- The oracle score lands almost exactly on your current score. The "perfect" step may never have been swapped in, so the app quietly ran its normal retrieval.
- The oracle score comes out lower than your current system. That isn't impossible, but it's a reason to look closer. The gold labels (the known right answers for each step, like correct document ids) may be wrong or missing for some questions.
- Some eval questions have no gold document ids at all. Then the oracle has nothing correct to hand over.

**Quickest check:** open a few traces from the oracle run in MLflow. A trace is the saved record of each step's inputs and outputs. Confirm the documents passed to `generate` match the gold ids for that question. Then confirm every row in `eval_set` has gold ids filled in.

judge.notes: The bullet saying an oracle score almost equal to the current score means the perfect step was probably never swapped in clashes with the lesson, where a small gain (78% to 80%) is a valid result showing that step has little headroom.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Steps affect each other.** Oracle runs make one step perfect at a time, but steps can depend on each other. Perfect reranking may barely help until retrieval finds the right documents at all. So also run a combined oracle, with two steps made perfect together, before you decide.

**2. A small eval set.** The eval set is your list of test questions. With only 50 of them, one answer flipping moves the score by 2 points, so small gaps can be pure luck. Add more questions, or rerun each variant a few times, and only trust gaps clearly bigger than that wobble.

**3. The right answers go stale or don't exist.** Oracle runs need the correct answer for each step, like the right document ids for each question, and those break when your documents change. Agents may have several valid tool paths, so there is no single correct tool result. Refresh these answers whenever the data changes, and for agents, write them only for the key tool calls.

learn:term.a:
**Design** and **Evaluate** are two stages of testing your app.

**Design** is planning, before anything runs. You choose the variants to test. A variant is one version of your app, like one with a new prompt. Here you also add oracle variants, such as `rag-oracle-retrieval`. You check that your eval set has the right answer for each step, like the correct document ids for each question.

**Evaluate** is reading results, after the runs finish. You read the oracle scores first, because they show where effort will pay off.

They depend on each other. Evaluate can only read what Design set up. If you skip an oracle run in Design, there's nothing to compare later.

Think of a doctor. Ordering the tests is Design. Reading the results is Evaluate.

In the lesson's example, the whole app scores 78%. When retrieval is swapped for the right documents, the whole app scores 91%. That 13-point gap is retrieval's headroom: the most you could gain by perfecting that step. Reranking's headroom is 6 points and the prompt's is 2. So you work on retrieval first.

judge.notes: The answer uses "oracle" (variants, scores, run) and "retrieval" and "reranking" without ever explaining them, so a beginner can't tell what an oracle variant is; the content is otherwise consistent with the lesson.

check:0:0.q: Why not “B is better: its top run is 0.84”?
check:0:0.a:
It gets one fact right. B's top run, 0.84, is the highest single score of all six runs.

But one run can't tell you much. LLM outputs and LLM judges (a model used to grade answers) vary from run to run. So any single score is partly luck. Picking each setup's best run means comparing their luckiest moments, not their typical performance.

Look at the full ranges instead:

- **A:** 0.80, 0.83, 0.81 → 0.80 to 0.83
- **B:** 0.82, 0.84, 0.80 → 0.80 to 0.84

B's worst run (0.80) does not beat A's best run (0.83). In fact, B's worst run ties A's worst run. The ranges overlap a lot. So there is no clear sign that B is really better.

Overlap doesn't prove they're equal, either. It just means this test can't separate them. You could choose on cost or speed, or test on more examples.

"No clear winner: the ranges overlap" is better because it judges each setup by all its runs, not by one lucky score.

check:0:2.q: Why not “A is better: its runs are steadier”?
check:0:2.a:
It gets one small thing right. A's scores do sit a bit closer together. A spans 0.80 to 0.83, a spread of 0.03. B spans 0.80 to 0.84, a spread of 0.04.

But it misses two things.

First, the lesson asks which prompt scores **higher**, not which one wobbles less. On that, A doesn't lead. Its average is about 0.81, while B's is 0.82. So "steadier" quietly swaps in a different question.

Second, a gap of 0.01 in spread, from only three runs, is itself likely to be luck. One more run could easily flip it. You'd be crowning a winner on noise, which is exactly the **false positive** (a fake winner) the lesson warns about.

Apply the rule instead. A's worst run (0.80) does not beat B's best (0.84). B's worst (0.80) does not beat A's best (0.83). The ranges overlap, so neither wins. Choose on cost or speed, or test on more examples.

"No clear winner: the ranges overlap" is better because it uses the lesson's actual test, worst run against best run, instead of guessing from a tiny, noisy difference.

check:1:1.a:
"Agreed: 0.82 beats 0.80" gets one thing right. On that single run, 0.82 really is the higher number. Your teammate read the scores correctly.

What it misses is that one run can't show you how much the scores wobble. LLM outputs change a little each time you run them. So does the LLM judge, which is a model that grades the answers. That random wobble is called noise.

Because of noise, A might score 0.79 on the next try and B might score 0.83. A gap of 0.02 is small enough to come from luck alone. You can't tell from one run whether A is truly better or just had a good roll of the dice.

Agreeing now could lead you to ship a "winner" that isn't really better. That mistake is a false positive: calling a difference real when it isn't.

"Run each a few times before deciding" is the better answer because repeated runs show each prompt's range of scores, so you only pick a winner when the ranges clearly don't overlap.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Test a third prompt to break the tie”?
check:1:2.a:
"Test a third prompt to break the tie" gets one thing right. It doesn't accept the teammate's claim that A wins. A gap of 0.02 from a single run each is too small to trust.

But it misreads the problem. There isn't really a tie to break. The real issue is **noise**, meaning the random wobble in scores from run to run. LLM outputs change between runs, and so do LLM judges (models that grade other models' answers). So 0.82 against 0.80 could easily flip if you ran them again.

Adding prompt C doesn't fix that. You'd get one more single score with the same wobble. It also tells you nothing about whether A truly beats B. Now you have three shaky numbers instead of two.

What you need is more runs of A and B, so you can see how much each one's score moves around. Then you check whether their ranges clearly separate. That means A's worst run should beat B's best run, or the other way round.

"Run each a few times before deciding" is better because it tackles the actual cause, run-to-run luck, and gives you ranges you can compare.

check:2:0.q: Why not “A, because it might be better”?
check:2:0.a:
"A, because it might be better" gets one thing right. Overlapping ranges don't prove the two setups are equal. A real difference could be hiding in the noise. The lesson calls that a **false negative**: missing a winner that really exists.

But the reasoning stops halfway. If A *might* be better, then B *might* be better too. Overlap means the runs gave you no reason to favour either one. Picking A is a guess, and it's a guess that costs twice as much.

It also skips the honest next step. If you truly suspect A is better, the fix is to gather more evidence. You could test on more examples, or use a **paired comparison**, which scores both setups on the same examples and is better at spotting small differences. Hoping isn't evidence, so it shouldn't decide the pick.

"B: no clear winner, so pick on cost" is better because, when quality can't be told apart, cost is the only difference you can actually measure, and B wins that clearly.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Neither: start the experiment over”?
check:2:2.a:
"Neither: start the experiment over" gets one thing right. Overlapping ranges mean you can't call a quality winner. It also senses that more data could help.

But it misses two things.

First, it throws away what you already know. Your runs didn't show a clear quality gap. The cost gap, though, is certain: B costs half as much. That is a solid reason to choose.

Second, redoing the same experiment may not settle much. Run the same setup again and the ranges may well overlap again. The lesson's advice is different. When ranges overlap, pick on cost or speed, or test on *more examples* (a bigger set of test inputs). It doesn't say to start from scratch.

One caution. Overlap doesn't prove A and B are equal in quality. A real gap might be hiding. Missing a real difference like that is called a **false negative**. If quality matters a lot, a paired comparison (next lesson) can check more closely.

"B: no clear winner, so pick on cost" is better because it makes a sensible decision now, based on the one difference you know is real.

explain:gotcha.a:
LLM outputs change from run to run. So do the scores from an LLM judge (a model that grades the answers). If you run each prompt only once, the gap you see may just be luck.

Here is how that bites in real work. You test prompt B once and it scores 0.84. Prompt A scored 0.80. You ship B. A week later, a teammate reruns both, and B scores 0.79. Nothing changed except chance. You spent time rolling out a "fix" that never helped. Worse, people start to distrust your evals.

"Fix what you can" means keeping everything else the same between the two setups: the same test examples, the same judge, the same scoring. Then the prompt is the only thing that differs.

Then run each setup several times. Three to five is common. In MLflow you can log each repeat as a nested run (a child run grouped under one parent run). Use a different seed each time. A seed is a number that controls the random choices. Changing it shows you the natural spread.

Only call a winner when the scores clearly separate. If they overlap, decide on cost or speed, or test on more examples.

judge.notes: The answer is about 225 words, over the roughly 200-word limit, and the MLflow nested-run and seed details add length the question did not need.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Worst run must beat best run” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "LLM outputs and LLM judges vary from run to run. So a single score of 0.82 against 0.80 might just be luck."

*The idea:* "I run each setup three to five times. I only call a winner if its worst run beats the other setup's best run. Think of two runners: one clearly wins only if their slowest race beats the other's fastest. If the score ranges overlap, I call it a tie. Then I choose on cost or speed, or I test on more examples."

*The trade-off:* "The rule is cautious. It rarely crowns a fake winner, which is called a false positive. But it can miss a real improvement, a false negative. Overlapping ranges don't prove the two setups are equal."

**Likely follow-up**

"How would you catch a small but real gain that this rule misses?"

*Hint for a strong answer:* Mention a **paired comparison**. If both setups ran on the same examples, you compare them example by example. This removes noise from some examples simply being easier than others, so it is more sensitive. Adding more examples or more runs also helps.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs that the lesson's idea was skipped:**

- **Only one score per setup.** In MLflow, the parent run has no nested runs under it. Nested runs are child runs grouped beneath one parent, one per repeat. So a winner was picked from a single try.
- **A tiny gap that flips.** Something like 0.82 against 0.80, and on a rerun the order swaps. That is noise, not a real gain.
- **A win that fades in real use.** The "better" prompt ships. Then quality drops back to the old level. The original win was probably luck.
- **Overlapping ranges called a win.** A range is a setup's lowest to highest score. Here, the setup that was crowned has a worst score below the other setup's best. That was really a tie.

**Quickest check:**

1. Open the parent run in MLflow and look at its child runs.
2. For each setup, note its lowest and highest score.
3. Ask one question: does the crowned setup's lowest score beat the other setup's highest?

If not, treat it as a tie. Choose on cost or speed, or test on more examples.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Comparing many setups at once.** Each pairwise check has about a 1 in 10 chance of a fake winner with 3 runs, so testing ten prompts makes a lucky "winner" likely. Pick a shortlist, then re-test the top one or two with fresh runs or more examples.

**2. A small but real gain.** If the true improvement is tiny, the ranges will often overlap, and this rule calls it a tie (a false negative, meaning a missed real win). Run both setups on the same examples and use a paired comparison, which the next lesson covers, or add more examples.

**3. Things change over time.** Hosted models get updated, and your data drifts (slowly shifts away from what you tested on). Runs from last month and runs from today aren't a fair comparison, so rerun both setups side by side, with the model version and data snapshot logged in MLflow.

learn:term.q: How is “false positive” different from “false negative”?
learn:term.a:
Both are mistakes the rule can make, but in opposite directions.

A **false positive** means calling a winner when there isn't one. The gap was just luck. For example, B scores 0.82 and A scores 0.80 in a single run, yet the two setups are really equally good.

A **false negative** means missing a real winner. One setup truly is better, but its range overlaps the other's, so the rule says "no clear winner." In the lesson, C and D overlap. D might really be better. The rule just can't tell from these runs.

An everyday comparison is a smoke alarm. A false positive is the alarm beeping when there's no fire. A false negative is the alarm staying silent during a real fire.

The two trade off against each other. A stricter rule cuts false positives but causes more false negatives. "Worst run must beat best run" is strict on purpose. It rarely crowns a fake winner: about 1 time in 10 with 3 runs each, and far less often with 5. The price is that it sometimes misses real gains. A paired comparison, covered in the next lesson, is more sensitive and helps catch those.

check:0:1.q: Why not “B: it reaches 0.95 on one fold”?
check:0:1.a:
It's true that Model B hit 0.95 on one fold. That number is real, and it shows B *can* do very well on some data.

But picking a model for its best fold brings back the problem cross-validation was meant to solve. One test set can be lucky. A single 0.95 might just be a fold full of easy examples. The whole point of using several folds is to stop trusting any one of them on its own.

Look at B's other scores too. It also dropped to 0.60 on a different fold. Once your model is live, you don't get to choose which kind of data arrives. Some days could look like that 0.60 fold. B's scores swing a lot, so its **standard deviation** (a measure of how far the scores spread from their average) is large. A's is zero.

Both models have the same average, 0.80. So the average can't break the tie. The spread is what decides it.

**A is the safer choice because it gives the same result on every fold, so you can trust it to behave the same way on new data.**

judge.notes: No significant problems. The closing claim that A will 'behave the same way on new data' is slightly stronger than the lesson supports, but it stays within a reasonable reading.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Neither: the averages are the same”?
check:0:2.a:
"Neither" gets one thing right. The averages really are equal. Both models come out at 0.80.

What it misses is the second number the lesson asks you to report: **how much the scores vary**. That's the **standard deviation**, a measure of how far the scores usually sit from their average.

Model A scores 0.80 on every fold. Its spread is zero. Model B jumps around: 0.95 on one fold, 0.60 on another. Each fold is a different slice of your data. So B's swings mean its quality depends a lot on which examples it happens to see.

Once a model is live, it meets new data you didn't pick. With B, you can't tell whether you'll get the 0.95 version or the 0.60 version. That's also why the lesson's code logs `f1_min`, the worst fold's score. A's worst is 0.80, but B's is 0.60.

Looking only at the average throws away exactly the information cross-validation was built to give you.

"A: it is steady on every fold" is better because, with equal averages, the steadier model is the one you can trust to perform the same way on data it hasn't seen yet.

judge.notes: Minor: 'That's also why the lesson's code logs f1_min' states a motivation the lesson never gives, and it uses f1_min without explaining it.

check:1:1.q: Why not “One split always scores too low”?
check:1:1.a:
"One split always scores too low" gets one thing right. It notices that a single train/test split can give you a misleading number. That instinct is good.

The problem is the word "always." A single split has no built-in bias in one direction. Which examples land in the test set is partly chance. Sometimes the test set happens to hold easy examples, and your score comes out too high. Sometimes it holds hard or unusual ones, and your score comes out too low. You can't tell which happened from one number alone.

So your 0.91 might be flattering you, or it might be underselling the model. The real issue is that one split gives you no sense of how much the score would wobble with a different split. Cross-validation fixes this. It tests on each fold in turn, so you get several scores. Their average tells you the typical score. Their spread, the standard deviation, tells you how much luck was involved.

"That split may have been lucky" is better because it names the real risk: chance can push one score away from the model's true performance.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Scores only count in production”?
check:1:2.a:
"Scores only count in production" has a grain of truth. Real users matter most. A model can look good in testing and still struggle once it's live, because real data can drift away from what you trained on. ("Production" means the model running for real users.)

But it misses the actual problem with the 0.91. It throws out offline testing completely. ("Offline" means testing on saved data before release.) You need those tests to pick a model before you ship anything. You can't send every candidate to real users just to see which one works.

The real issue is narrower. One train/test split is one random cut of your data. By chance, the test set might hold easy examples, and you get a high score. A different cut might give 0.84. One number can't tell you which kind of cut you got.

That's why cross-validation tests on every fold in turn and reports the average and the spread.

"That split may have been lucky" is better because it names the real flaw: one split is one random draw, and cross-validation fixes that.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Nothing, 5 folds each is fair”?
check:2:0.a:
"Nothing, 5 folds each is fair" gets one thing right. Both models had the same *number* of tries, and each try tested on unseen data. That part is fair.

What it misses is *which* examples ended up in each fold. Some examples are easy to classify and some are hard. If model A happened to be tested on folds full of easy emails, and model B on folds with more tricky ones, A looks better. That gap comes from the luck of the split, not from A being smarter. That is the exact "lucky or unlucky split" problem cross-validation is meant to reduce. Using different folds lets it sneak back in.

With the same folds, you can also compare the two models fold by fold. Fold 0 against fold 0, fold 1 against fold 1, and so on. If one model wins on most folds, you can trust the difference more than a gap in the averages alone. Logging both as MLflow runs, with the same fold setup recorded, keeps that comparison reproducible.

**Why "Run both on the same folds" is better:** it makes the test data identical for both models, so any difference in score comes from the models themselves, not from the split.

judge.notes: No real problem. The answer runs to about 200 words, and the fold-by-fold comparison goes slightly beyond the lesson without contradicting it.

check:2:1.a:
"Use 10 folds each instead" isn't wrong as a setting. Ten folds is a normal choice for cross-validation. But it doesn't fix the problem in the question.

The problem is that each model got its own set of folds. A **fold** is one group of examples that takes a turn as the test set. If model A and model B are tested on different groups, one might get easier examples just by chance. Then a better score could come from the split, not the model.

Switching to 10 folds keeps that problem. Each model would still get its own 10 folds, so they'd still be tested on different examples. You'd have changed the number of folds, not the fairness of the comparison.

**"Run both on the same folds"** is the right answer. It means both models are trained and tested on exactly the same examples in each round, so the data split is no longer one of the things that differs between them.

judge.notes: The claim that ten folds is a normal choice goes slightly beyond the lesson, which only says 'often 5', but it doesn't contradict it. Otherwise the answer is accurate, within the word limit, and gives no exercise solution.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Round-robin: deal examples out like cards” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

**The problem:** "One train/test split can be lucky or unlucky. A model might look great just because the test set happened to be easy."

**The idea:** "Cross-validation splits the data into groups called folds. Each fold takes one turn as the test set, and the model trains on the rest. To build the folds, I deal example numbers out like cards around a table: example 0 to fold 0, example 1 to fold 1, and so on, then wrap back to fold 0. That's round-robin. The remainder `i % num_folds` tells me which fold each example lands in."

**The edge case:** "If the examples don't divide evenly, some folds get one extra. With 10 examples and 3 folds, the sizes are 4, 3 and 3. That's fine. Sizes never differ by more than one."

**A likely follow-up**

*"What if you have fewer examples than folds?"*

Hint: some folds would end up empty. A test on an empty fold gives no real score. A strong answer says you'd check for this first. Then either stop with a clear error or use fewer folds.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs in your numbers**

- **Only one score.** If a model reports a single number with no spread, it probably came from one train/test split. That split may have been lucky. The score then drops in real use, or changes a lot when you split again.
- **Big spread across folds.** Five scores like 0.91, 0.62, 0.88, 0.70, 0.95 mean results depend heavily on which examples land in the test set. The average alone hides this. The **standard deviation** (how far scores typically sit from the average) shows it.
- **Winners that flip.** If model A beats B, then loses on a rerun, they may have been tested on different folds.
- **No MLflow run per model.** You can't reproduce or compare results later.

**Warning signs in the folds themselves**

- An example appears in two folds, or in none.
- Fold sizes differ by more than one.
- A round's test examples also show up in its training set. That is a leak, and scores look too good.

**Quickest check**

For each round, list the test examples and the training examples. Confirm there is no overlap and that every example is tested exactly once. Then open MLflow and check that each model has its own run, with a mean and a spread from the same folds.

learn:stops.a:
Cross-validation works well when examples are independent and the model is trained on your data. Here are three cases where it needs care.

**Data that changes over time.** For fraud or churn, dealing examples out like cards mixes future data into training. The model then "sees the future" and scores look better than real life. Instead, split by time: train on older months and test on the next month, then roll forward.

**Related examples.** If one customer has many rows, some can land in training and others in testing. The model memorises that customer, which is a form of **leakage** (test information sneaking into training). Keep each customer's rows together in one fold.

**LLM or RAG apps.** You usually don't train these, so there is nothing to retrain per fold. Instead, build a fixed set of test questions with expected answers. Score every version on that same set, and log each version as an MLflow run.

learn:term.a:
**Folds** are the pieces. **Cross-validation** is the method that uses those pieces.

A **fold** is just a group of examples. You split your data into a few equal groups, often 5. On their own, folds do nothing. They are just piles.

**Cross-validation** is the whole process. It takes turns: each fold gets one round as the test set, while all the other folds are used for training. Every round gives a score. At the end you report the average score and how much the scores vary (the **standard deviation**, a measure of spread).

An everyday comparison: folds are like dividing a class into 5 study groups. Cross-validation is the rotation where each group takes a turn presenting while the others listen.

In the lesson's example, 10 examples become 5 folds: fold 0 holds examples 0 and 5, fold 1 holds 1 and 6, and so on. That's the splitting. Then cross-validation runs 5 rounds. Round 1 tests on fold 0 and trains on folds 1 to 4. Round 2 tests on fold 1, and so on. That gives 5 scores.

So you need folds to do cross-validation. Cross-validation is what turns them into a fair test.

judge.notes: No major problem; the 'presenting while others listen' analogy is loose, since the presenting group is the test set, but it does not contradict the lesson.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Ship it: the quality win is clear”?
check:0:0.a:
"Ship it" gets one thing right. The quality win is real. With 15 wins and 5 losses, the gap is 10. The bar is twice the square root of 20, which is about 8.9. So 10 clears it, and the paired check would say "clearly better."

But the rule never gets that far. Gates come first. A **gate** is a must-hold condition: if it fails, the answer is no, whatever else looks good. A must-pass case is exactly that kind of condition. One of them now fails, so the gate fails.

Choosing "ship" here means letting a good number in one place outweigh a hard "no" in another. That is the cherry-picking the decision rule exists to stop. Think of the job offer again. A great team doesn't matter if the salary is below your minimum.

The quality win isn't wasted, though. Fix the failing case, rerun, and the new version may well ship next round.

"Keep the baseline: a gate failed" is better because it follows the rule in its fixed order: any failed gate means no, and the failed gate is saved as the reason.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Too close to call: one case is not much”?
check:0:2.a:
That option has one thing right. "Too close to call" keeps the baseline for now, so the version you run in production would be the same. But the reason it gives is wrong, and the saved reasons matter.

It misses two things.

First, a must-pass case is a **gate**. A gate is a yes-or-no check that must hold, or the answer is no. It doesn't matter that only one case failed. One failure is enough. The size of the failure isn't part of the rule.

Second, quality isn't close at all. There are 15 wins and 5 losses, so the gap is 10. The bar is twice the square root of 20, which is about 8.9. A gap of 10 clears it, so on quality alone the new version clearly wins. But the rule never gets that far. Gates come first, and one failed.

"Too close to call" also tells the team to gather more examples. More examples won't fix a broken must-pass case.

"Keep the baseline: a gate failed" is better because it follows the rule in order and saves the true reason: fix that case first.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Only the first gate that failed”?
check:1:0.a:
"Only the first gate that failed" gets one thing right. The decision itself would be correct. Any single failed gate means the answer is no, so you would still say "keep baseline". Stopping at the first failure doesn't change that.

What it misses is the full picture. Say the report only mentions the cost. The team works on cost, runs the comparison again, and only then learns that a must-pass case also fails. That is a second round of fixing they could have avoided. The lesson's advice is to check every gate and list each one that fails, so the team can fix them all in one round.

There is a second reason. The reasons are saved with the decision. A reviewer reads that list, and so will you in six months. If one failure is left out, the record is incomplete, and nobody reading it later would know the must-pass case failed.

"Both failed gates" is better because it gives the team and any later reader every reason for "no" at once, so all the problems can be fixed together.

check:1:2.a:
"The quality score first" gets one thing right: quality does matter. It is part of the decision rule.

But it comes at the wrong time. The rule checks the **gates** first. Gates are the must-hold conditions: every must-pass case passes, cost per task is within budget, and p95 latency is within budget. Here two gates fail. So the answer is already "keep baseline". No quality score can change that.

Leading with quality also brings back the problem the rule exists to stop. A strong score up front makes it tempting to argue past the failures, for example "it's so much better, surely the cost is fine." Picking the number that favours the version you hoped would win is exactly what a fixed order prevents.

There is a practical cost too. The team needs to know *what to fix*. A quality score does not tell them that. A list of failed gates does.

"Both failed gates" is better because it shows the real reasons for "keep baseline", both the cost and the must-pass case, so the team can fix everything in one round.

judge.notes: No major problems; the only small point is that 'p95 latency' is mentioned without a short explanation, though it isn't central to this case.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Ship it: every gate passed”?
check:2:0.a:
"Ship it: every gate passed" gets one thing right. The gates did pass, so the new version is allowed to compete. Nothing rules it out.

What it misses is what gates are for. A gate can only say no. Passing one means "not disqualified," not "better." Think of the job offer: the salary clearing your minimum doesn't mean you take the job. It just means you go on to compare the rest.

The next step in the rule is the quality check. Here, wins minus losses was not big enough to count as clearly better. So the numbers don't show the new version beats the old one. Shipping now would mean switching on a hunch. That is exactly what the fixed rule is meant to stop.

"Too close to call" has its own planned outcome. You keep what already works, then gather more examples or decide on cost. You save that reason with the decision.

"Keep the baseline for now" is better because you only switch when the evidence shows the new version is better, and here it doesn't.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Drop the new version for good”?
check:2:1.a:
"Drop the new version for good" gets one thing right. You do not ship the new version today. The baseline stays in place.

But it reads "too close to call" as "the new version lost." Those are different results. "Too close" means the gap between wins and losses was smaller than twice the square root of wins plus losses. In plain words, the test could not tell the two versions apart. It did not find the new version worse. The rule has a separate outcome for that, "keep baseline" because it is clearly worse.

Remember too that this candidate passed every gate. All must-pass cases passed, and cost and speed were within budget. A version like that is worth another look. More examples might show a real gap. Or you might pick it because it is cheaper. Dropping it for good throws that chance away on evidence that never said no.

"Keep the baseline for now" is better because it stays safe today while leaving room for more examples, or a choice based on cost, to settle the question later.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Gates first, then one test” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem.* "A model comparison gives me several numbers: quality, must-pass cases, cost and speed. Look at each one alone and I can usually find one that makes my favourite version win."

*The idea.* "So I write one rule before I run anything. First the gates. These are hard limits: every must-pass case passes, cost per task is within budget, and p95 latency is within budget. p95 means 95 out of 100 requests are faster than that. If any gate fails, we keep the baseline, which is the current version. I list every failed gate, not just the first. Only if all pass do I compare quality with a paired check: wins against losses on the same questions."

*The trade-off.* "A big quality gain still loses if it breaks a gate. And a small gap is 'too close to call', so we keep the baseline for now."

**A likely follow-up**

"Why fix the order before you run the evaluation?"

Hint: say it stops you choosing the rule after seeing the results. Logging the reasons with the decision also makes it easy for a reviewer, or you in six months, to check.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The reason changes every time.** One release ships "because quality went up", the next "because it's cheaper". That suggests someone picked the number that favoured their version after seeing the results.
- **A gate failed but it shipped anyway.** For example, p95 latency was over budget. (p95 latency means 95 out of 100 requests are faster than this time.) If good quality talked the team past a failed gate, the gates were not really gates.
- **Fixes arrive one at a time.** The team fixes cost, then learns latency also failed. Only the first failing gate was reported.
- **"Too close to call" never appears.** Every decision is a confident "ship" or "keep", even on tiny gaps in wins and losses.
- **Decisions have no reasons.** A logged "ship" with no list of why leaves reviewers guessing.

**Quickest check**

Open the saved decision record in MLflow, such as `decision.json`. Does it name the rule, and was that rule written before the evaluation run? Then redo the decision by hand from the logged numbers. Check each gate against its budget. Then do the paired check on wins and losses. If your answer differs from the logged one, the rule was skipped.

judge.notes: Mostly fine. The check asks whether the rule was written before the run, but decision.json only names the rule and can't show timing. "Gates" and "paired check" are also not re-explained, and the length is right at the limit.

learn:stops.a:
The rule works well, but three situations need extra care.

**Very little data.** The paired check only counts questions where the two versions disagree. With just a handful of those, almost nothing clears "twice the square root." Say 3 wins and 0 losses: 3 is less than twice the square root of 3, about 3.5, so the answer is still too close to call. Gather more examples, or decide on cost.

**Data that changes over time.** Real user questions drift away from your test set. A version can pass every gate on old examples and still fail on today's traffic. Refresh your examples regularly, add new must-pass cases from real failures, and review the budgets too.

**An LLM grading the answers.** In an LLM or RAG app (one that looks up documents before answering), a second model often decides "right" or "wrong." That judge is a bit random, so wins and losses can flip on a rerun. Spot-check the judge against human grades. Grade each answer more than once and keep the majority result.

judge.notes: Minor: the small-data and LLM-judge items run to four sentences, over the requested two or three, and LLM is not spelled out. Neither breaks a check.

learn:term.q: How is “ship” different from “keep the baseline”?
learn:term.a:
**Ship** means you switch to the new version. **Keep the baseline** means you stay with the version you already run (the "baseline"). They are the two firm answers your rule can give.

The difference is what it takes to reach each one. To ship, the new version must pass every gate, the checks that must hold. Then it must clearly win on quality, judged by the paired check. On the same questions, you count the ones only the new version got right (wins) and only the old one got right (losses). Wins must beat losses by a clear margin.

Keeping the baseline is the safe default. Any failed gate leads there. So does the new version clearly losing. Even "too close to call" keeps it for now.

Think of replacing your car. You buy the new one only if it fits your budget and is clearly better. Otherwise you keep the old one.

In the lesson's example, the candidate passes the must-pass cases and cost. Its p95 latency is 2.1 s, but the budget is 1.5 s. (p95 means 95 out of 100 requests are faster than this.) So the answer is keep baseline, because: too slow.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Yes: 4 points is a clear gain”?
check:0:0.a:
"Yes: 4 points is a clear gain" gets one thing right. Prompt B really did score higher on this eval set. That 4-point gap is real in the numbers you measured.

What it misses is how rough those numbers are. With 100 questions, the margin of error is about 10 points either way. The margin of error is how far a measured score could be from the real pass rate. So if A scored 70, its real rate could be anywhere from about 60 to 80. B's score has the same wide range.

A 4-point gap fits easily inside that range. Random luck in which questions happened to be in the set could produce a gap that size even if both prompts are equally good. So 4 points is not "clear." It is too small for this eval set to tell apart from noise.

To show a gap that small, you would need more examples, or a comparison on the same examples, which is more sensitive.

"Not on its own: the gap is inside the margin" is better because it checks the gap against the margin of error before trusting it.

check:0:2.q: Why not “No: an eval can't compare two prompts”?
check:0:2.a:
That option gets one thing right. You shouldn't conclude that B is better from this result. But it gives the wrong reason.

Comparing prompts is one of the main jobs of an eval. Run both prompts on a test set and see which scores higher. That's normal. The method is fine. The problem here is the **sample size**, meaning how many questions you tested on.

With 100 questions, each score has a **margin of error** of about 10 points either way. The margin is how far the measured score could be from the real pass rate. A 4-point gap is much smaller than that. So the gap could just be luck in which questions happened to be in the set.

Change the setup and the same eval could settle it. With 1,600 questions the margin is about 2.5 points, so a 4-point gap would stand out. Comparing both prompts on the same examples also helps. That method is coming later in this module, and it's more sensitive.

"Not on its own: the gap is inside the margin" is better because it names the real problem: too few examples for a gap this small, not evals themselves.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Yes, any change will show up”?
check:1:0.a:
**What it gets right:** a change to your prompt or model usually does move the score. Run the eval again and you will likely see a different number.

**What it misses:** a different number is not the same as a real improvement. With only 25 questions, the margin of error is about 20 points either way. The margin of error is how far your measured score could be from the true pass rate. A real 70% could show up as anything from about 50% to 90%, just from which questions happened to be in the set.

So a 3-point gain is buried in that 20-point wobble. Your score could go up by 3, down by 10, or up by 15, and you could not tell whether the change caused it or chance did.

There is a second catch. With 25 questions, each question is worth 4 points. One extra pass already moves the score by more than the 3 points you hope to see.

**Why "No, the margin of error is too wide" is better:** the hoped-for gain of 3 points is far smaller than the roughly 20-point margin, so this eval set cannot separate a real improvement from random noise.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Yes, if you run it twice”?
check:1:2.a:
**"Yes, if you run it twice"** has a sensible instinct behind it. More measuring usually means less guessing. And if your model gives slightly different answers each time (some randomness in how it writes), a second run can smooth that wobble out a little.

But it misses where the margin of error comes from. The margin is wide because you only have 25 questions. Those 25 are a small slice of all the questions real users might ask. A different 25 could easily score quite differently.

Running the same 25 questions twice doesn't add new questions. You're still looking through the same small slice. If the model answers the same way each time, you'll just get the same score twice.

With 25 examples, the margin is about plus or minus 20 points. A hoped-for gain of 3 points is far smaller than that. It would be lost in the noise either way. To see it, you need many more *different* examples, or a comparison of both versions on the same examples.

**"No, the margin of error is too wide"** is better because it names the real limit: 25 examples give a margin of about 20 points, far bigger than the 3-point change you want to spot.

judge.notes: No real problems. The run-to-run randomness point is not in the lesson but does not contradict it, and the length is right at the roughly 200-word limit.

check:2:1.a:
"About 200" gets one thing right: more questions do shrink the margin of error. It just assumes the shrinking happens at a steady rate. Double the questions, halve the margin. That feels natural, but it isn't how it works.

The margin shrinks with the **square root** of the number of questions. A square root is the number that, multiplied by itself, gives you the original. For example, the square root of 400 is 20, because 20 × 20 = 400.

The lesson's rule is: margin ≈ 100 divided by the square root of the number of questions.

- 100 questions: square root is 10, so 100 ÷ 10 = about 10 points.
- 200 questions: square root is about 14, so 100 ÷ 14 = about 7 points.
- 400 questions: square root is 20, so 100 ÷ 20 = about 5 points.

So doubling to 200 gets you from 10 points to about 7. That is better, but not the 5 you wanted. Each extra question helps a little less than the one before.

"About 400 questions" is better because halving the margin takes four times the examples, and 4 × 100 = 400.

check:2:2.a:
"About 110 questions" gets one thing right. More questions do shrink the margin of error. Adding examples is the right move.

What it misses is how slowly the margin shrinks. The margin doesn't fall in step with the number of questions. It falls with the square root. The square root of a number is the value that, multiplied by itself, gives that number. For example, the square root of 400 is 20.

Using the lesson's rule, the margin is about 100 divided by the square root of the number of questions:

- 100 questions: 100 ÷ 10 = about 10 points
- 110 questions: 100 ÷ about 10.5 = about 9.5 points
- 400 questions: 100 ÷ 20 = about 5 points

So 110 questions barely moves you. You'd still be about 9.5 points off, nowhere near 5.

This is why the lesson's rule of thumb says halving the margin takes four times the examples, not twice. Adding just 10% more questions is far too little.

"About 400 questions" is better because four times the examples is exactly what it takes to cut a 10-point margin down to about 5.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Run the margin rule backwards” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer**

*The problem.* An eval score is a rough guess. With few examples, the real pass rate could sit far from it. That gap is the margin of error.

*The idea.* So I start from the margin I can accept and work back to how many examples I need. The margin shrinks with the square root of the size. The square root is the number that, multiplied by itself, gives the size. In practice, halving the margin takes four times the examples. About 100 examples gives roughly 10 points either way. About 400 gives roughly 5. If the gain I hope to see is smaller than the margin, my eval set can't show it.

*The edge case.* The margin is widest near a 50% pass rate, so this rule gives safe planning numbers. Near 0% or 100% it breaks down. There I'd switch to a method built for extreme scores.

**A likely follow-up**

"What if you can't afford 400 examples?"

*Hint:* Run both versions on the same examples and compare them question by question. That is more sensitive, so smaller gains show up with fewer examples.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs your eval set is too small:**

- **Scores wobble with no real change.** You rerun the same prompt, or swap in a few fresh questions, and the pass rate moves by 5 or 10 points.
- **Small "wins" that vanish.** Prompt B beats prompt A by 3 points on 50 questions. You ship it, and in real use nobody can tell the difference.
- **A score that looks too good.** 90% on 20 questions, then it drops once real users arrive. With so few examples, luck can easily add or remove 20 points.
- **Missing numbers in MLflow.** Your runs log a score but no `n_examples` or `margin_points`. Then nobody can tell whether a gap between two runs is real.

**Quickest check:** look up the size of your eval set and work out its margin. The margin is 100 divided by the square root of the number of examples. So 100 examples gives about 10 points either way. Now compare that margin to the gap between your two scores. If the gap is smaller than the margin, the gap could be pure luck. Add more examples before you trust it.

learn:stops.a:
The rule works when examples are separate, random draws and the score sits somewhere in the middle. Here are three places it needs care.

**Scores near 0% or 100%.** At 49 out of 50, the rule's range can spill past 100%, which makes no sense. Use a **Wilson interval** there instead. It is a better formula for extreme scores, covered two lessons from now.

**Examples that aren't really separate.** In a RAG app (one that looks up documents before answering), you might write ten questions about the same document. They tend to pass or fail together, so they count for less than ten. Your true margin is wider than the rule says. Use the bootstrap, but draw whole groups (all questions from one document) instead of single questions.

**Real questions that change over time.** The margin only covers luck in which examples you picked. It says nothing about **drift**, which means users start asking different things than your eval set holds. Refresh the set from recent real questions so it still matches what people actually ask.

judge.notes: No real problems. Drawing whole groups in the bootstrap goes slightly beyond the lesson, but it doesn't contradict it.

learn:term.q: What does “margin of error” mean here?
learn:term.a:
**Margin of error** is how far your measured score could be from the real score, in either direction.

Think of tasting soup. One spoonful gives you a rough idea of how salty the whole pot is. But that spoonful might have a bit more or less salt than average. Taste more spoonfuls and your guess gets closer to the truth.
