Your eval set works the same way. The questions you test on are a sample of all the questions your agent could ever face. The pass rate you get is a guess about the real pass rate, not the truth itself.

In the lesson's example:

- Test on 100 questions and score 70%. The margin is about 10 **points** (a point is one question in every 100). So the real pass rate is probably somewhere from 60% to 80%.
- With 400 questions, the margin shrinks to about 5 points. Now the range is 65% to 75%.
- With only 25 questions, it's about 20 points. That's a very wide range.

That's why the MLflow snippet logs `margin_points` next to each score. A score only means much when you know how far off it could be.

check:0:0.q: Why not “The smaller chunk size helped”?
check:0:0.a:
"The smaller chunk size helped" is a natural guess. It gets one thing right: you did change `chunk_size` (how big each piece of a document is when it's split up for searching), and run B did score 6 points higher. The smaller chunks *might* be the reason.

What it misses is the second change. Run B also used index `v8` instead of `v7`. The index is the searchable copy of your documents. Maybe `v8` has new or cleaner documents. That alone could explain the 6 points.

So there are several possible stories:

- The smaller chunks helped.
- The new index helped.
- Both helped a bit.
- The smaller chunks actually hurt, but the new index helped even more.

The two runs can't tell these apart. Picking "the smaller chunk size helped" claims an answer the data doesn't support. That's what a confound does: it turns the result into non-evidence.

"Nothing yet: rerun B on index v7" is better because it admits you can't tell yet, and it fixes the problem by making `chunk_size` the only thing that differs between the runs.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Index v8 helped, so switch to it”?
check:0:2.a:
"Index v8 helped" gets one thing right: it notices that the index changed, and that change might matter.

But it jumps to a conclusion. Two things changed between run A and run B. First, `chunk_size` went from 512 to 256. That setting controls how big each piece of text is when the documents are cut up. Second, the index went from `v7` to `v8`. The index is the searchable copy of the documents that the app looks things up in.

The 6-point gain could come from the smaller chunks, the new index, or both together. It is even possible that `v8` made things worse and the smaller chunks made up for it. Giving all the credit to the index is a guess, not a finding. This result shows only that the two changes together scored higher.

"Nothing yet: rerun B on index v7" is better because it puts the index back to match run A, which leaves `chunk_size` as the only difference, so the next result actually means something.

check:1:1.q: Why not “A fair test: the name stayed the same”?
check:1:1.a:
"A fair test: the name stayed the same" gets one thing right. On paper, the runs do match. MLflow shows the same settings for A and B, including the same model name. So if you only look at the logged parameters, it looks fair.

What it misses is that a name is just a label. The provider can swap the actual model behind that label at any time. Your logs said the model stayed the same, but the thing doing the answering changed. A fair test needs the real controls to match, not just their labels.

So the lower score in run B is not evidence about anything you did. It might be the new model. You can't tell, because a setting moved that you didn't plan and didn't record.

The lesson's fix applies here. Log a pinned version of the model, meaning a specific dated release that won't change under you, not just its general name. Then a swap would show up when you compare the two runs' settings.

"A confound: a control quietly moved" is better because it names what really happened: something you meant to hold steady changed without you knowing, so the comparison no longer counts.

judge.notes: No real problems. The 'specific dated release that won't change under you' wording goes slightly beyond the lesson, which only says to log the model version, and the length is right at the limit.

check:1:2.q: Why not “A bug in how MLflow logs runs”?
check:1:2.a:
It's a fair first guess. MLflow showed two runs with matching settings, yet the scores were very different. So it's natural to suspect the record-keeping.

But MLflow did its job. It logged exactly what it was given. Both runs really did use the same model *name*, so the logged value really was the same. Nothing was recorded wrongly.

The change happened outside your code and outside MLflow. The provider (the company that serves the model) swapped the model behind that name. Run B used different model behaviour from run A. That's a second thing that changed without you planning it. That's the definition of a confound.

The lesson here is not "MLflow is broken." It's "I didn't log a setting that mattered." The name alone wasn't enough. Logging a pinned version would have shown the difference. A pinned version is a specific dated model ID instead of a general name.

"A confound: a control quietly moved" is better because it names the real problem. An unplanned change outside your code means the score gap tells you nothing about anything you did.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the 'pinned dated model ID' explanation goes slightly beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Rebuild the index before every run”?
check:2:0.a:
"Rebuild the index before every run" sounds careful, and it does get one thing right. Each run gets a clean, complete index (the searchable copy of the documents), with nothing half-built or stale.

The problem is what goes into each rebuild. New documents arrive every day, so a rebuild on Monday and a rebuild on Friday hold different documents. The index quietly changes between runs. That is a confound: a second thing that changed without you planning it.

Say run B scores better than run A. Was it your planned change, like `chunk_size`? Or were the answers just in the new documents? You can't tell. You end up measuring the documents, not your change.

Being up to date matters for a live app. In an experiment, it works against you. What you need is for everything except your one planned change to stay exactly the same.

Building the index once from a fixed copy is better because every run then searches the same documents, under one logged version like `index=v7`, so any difference in results comes from the one thing you changed.

judge.notes: Minor: the 'clean, complete index' and 'up to date matters for a live app' points come from outside the lesson, but they do not contradict it.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Only run on days with no new files”?
check:2:1.a:
**It gets one thing right.** It notices that new documents are a confound, a second change that could explain the difference instead of the change you planned.

**But it doesn't actually stop the documents from changing.** Say run A happens on a quiet day in week one, and run B on a quiet day in week two. Each day had no new files. But files arrived on the days in between. So the two runs still searched different sets of documents. You'd be measuring the documents, not your change.

**It also puts your experiment at the mercy of luck.** If files arrive every day, you may get very few quiet days, or none at all. Then you can't run the experiment.

**Why "Build the index once from a fixed copy" is better:** freezing one copy of the documents, giving that index a version, and logging the version with every run keeps the documents identical across all runs, no matter what arrives during the two weeks. (The index is the searchable copy of your documents that the app looks things up in.)

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Compare two dicts key by key” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem.* "A comparison between two runs only counts as evidence if the one thing I planned to change is the only thing that changed. Any other setting that moved is a confound, a hidden second cause."

*The idea.* "I treat each run's settings as a dict, a list of name–value pairs. I walk through every name that appears in either run. I skip the one I planned to change. I flag any name whose values differ, and I sort the flagged names so the report is easy to read."

*The edge case.* "A setting that is missing from one run still counts as a difference. If run B logged `judge` and run A didn't, I can't prove they match, so I flag it."

**Likely follow-up**

"What if two values look different but mean the same thing?"

*Hint:* MLflow stores parameters as text. So `5` and `5.0`, or `0.50` and `0.5`, won't match. A strong answer has two parts. First, log every setting in one consistent format. Second, decide on purpose whether to clean values up before comparing. Flagging too much is safer than missing a real confound.

judge.notes: No major problems. The claim that MLflow stores parameters as text is not in the lesson, though it does not contradict it. The answer also retells the comparison steps in words, but it gives no code and no Check answer.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **A big jump from a small change.** You nudged `chunk_size` and the score leapt. Tiny changes rarely cause huge effects. Something else probably moved.
- **The win won't repeat.** You rerun the "better" version later and the gain shrinks or vanishes.
- **Your baseline drifts.** You rerun the old, unchanged version and get a different score than before. The setup moved under you.
- **The eval looks different.** The question count changed, or every answer's score shifted at once, which points to a new judge model (the model that grades answers).
- **It fails in real use.** The score looked great, then dropped once real users arrived. The test conditions didn't match reality.

**Quickest check**

Open both runs in MLflow and compare their logged parameters side by side. Only the one setting you planned should differ. Watch for settings logged in one run but missing from the other.

If a setting was never logged, like the index version or judge version, you can't rule it out. Treat the result as unproven. Then rerun both versions on the same frozen setup.

learn:stops.a:
**When this stops working**

**1. The setting looks the same, but isn't.** A provider can update the model behind the same name, like `gpt-4o`. Your parameter diff shows no change, yet answers shift. Pin a dated model version where you can, and log the exact version string the provider returns.

**2. A setting was never logged.** The diff only sees what you logged. A prompt edited in a file, a new library version, or a changed system message stays invisible. Log every setting that could matter, including package versions and a fingerprint of the prompt text. A fingerprint (called a hash) is a short code that changes whenever the text changes.

**3. Only one thing changed, but the result is still noisy.** With temperature above zero, or a small eval set, two runs of the *same* setup can score differently. The gap you see might just be chance. Repeat each run a few times, use a larger eval set, and only trust differences bigger than that run-to-run wobble.

learn:term.a:
A **confound** is a second thing that changed between two runs without you planning it.

**An everyday comparison.** Say you try a new plant food to see if your plant grows faster. That same week, you also move the pot to a sunnier window. The plant grows faster. Was it the food or the sun? You can't tell. The sun is the confound. It moved quietly, and now your result says nothing clear about the food.

**In the lesson's example.** The planned change is `chunk_size`, which is how big each piece of a document is when it gets stored. Run A uses `512` and run B uses `256`. So far, so good.

Now look at the other settings:

- `k` (how many pieces get looked up) is `5` in both runs, so it matches.
- `judge` (the model that grades answers) is `j2` in both runs, so it matches.
- `index` (the searchable copy of the documents) is `v7` in run A but `v8` in run B.

That `index` difference is the confound. If run B scores better, the cause could be the smaller chunks or the rebuilt index. The comparison can't settle which one it was.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Ship it: it won clearly on the dev set”?
check:0:0.a:
"Ship it" gets one thing right. A clear win on the dev set is a real signal, and that variant is the right one to look at more closely.

What it misses is how many tries it took to get there. You tested 15 variants. Each one has about a 5% chance of "winning" by pure luck, which is called a **false positive**. Across 15 tries, the chance that at least one is a fluke falls between the 40% and 64% shown in the lesson's table. That is a lot.

There is a second problem. You picked the best of many, so its dev score is partly luck. That number is too optimistic. This is the **multiple comparisons problem**: the more you try, the more likely the top result looks better than it really is.

So a clear win on the same data you used to choose it doesn't prove much.

"Confirm it once on the holdout set" is better because the holdout examples were kept aside and never used to pick the winner, so a single test there gives an honest score that luck in the search can't inflate.

judge.notes: Minor: calling the dev win 'a real signal' slightly overstates it, since the lesson says the best of many is partly luck, but the answer corrects this later.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Try 15 more variants to be sure”?
check:0:2.a:
The instinct behind "Try 15 more variants to be sure" is good. You doubt the win and want more evidence before shipping. That caution is right.

The problem is that this option does the opposite of what you want. Every extra variant is another comparison, and each comparison has its own 5% chance of a lucky win, a **false positive**. With 15 variants, the odds that at least one won by luck are already about one in two. Adding 15 more pushes those odds even higher.

It also never tests the winner itself. You would be running more contests on the same **dev set**, the examples you have been tuning on. The best of 30 is still partly luck, and its dev score is still too optimistic.

What you actually need is a fresh, fair look at the one prompt you picked.

**Confirm it once on the holdout set** is the better answer. The holdout examples were never used to choose the winner, so a single check there shows whether the win was real or a fluke.

check:1:0.q: Why not “20 prompts is too few to try”?
check:1:0.a:
"20 prompts is too few to try" points the wrong way. The problem is not that the teammate tried too few. Trying more prompts would make it worse, not better.

What it gets right is small: the number of prompts does matter. But each extra prompt is one more chance for a lucky win. With 20 prompts, the chance that at least one "wins" by luck is already about 64%. With 50, it climbs even higher.

What it misses is the real mistake. The teammate picked the best score on the dev set, the examples used while building, and then quoted that same score as a forecast. The best of many is partly luck, so that number is too optimistic. Production will likely look worse.

The fix is not more prompts. It is to confirm the winner once on the holdout set, the examples kept aside that it has never seen. That gives an honest score.

"The best of 20 is partly luck" is better because it names the actual flaw: picking the top score from many tries inflates it, so it can't be trusted as a prediction.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Dev-set scores always run low”?
check:1:1.a:
"Dev-set scores always run low" gets one thing right. It senses that the quoted number is not a fair forecast of production. That instinct is good.

But it points the wrong way. The **dev set** is the batch of examples you use while trying out variants. When you try 20 prompts on it and keep the top scorer, that score tends to run *high*, not low. Some of the winner's lead came from luck: it happened to suit those particular examples. In production it meets new examples, and that lucky boost fades.

The word "always" is also off. Dev scores are not low or high by nature. The problem comes from *picking the best of many* on the same set. Test one prompt and its dev score is a fair estimate. Test twenty and keep the top one, and the estimate becomes too rosy.

The fix is to check the winner once on the **holdout set**, examples it has never seen, and quote that score instead.

"The best of 20 is partly luck" is the better answer because it names the real cause: choosing the top scorer out of many inflates its score.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Run all 50 on the holdout set”?
check:2:0.a:
"Run all 50 on the holdout set" gets one thing right. The holdout set is the honest test. It holds examples kept aside that no variant has seen, so its scores are not inflated by tuning.

The problem is how often it gets used. The holdout set is meant for one job: confirming a single winner, once. If all 50 prompts run on it, you are back to picking the best of many. That best score is partly luck, just as before. The multiple comparisons problem has simply moved to a new place.

With 50 comparisons at the usual 5% bar, a lucky "win" is very likely. That is even more likely than the 64% the lesson shows for 20. Once you have picked a winner off the holdout set, you have no clean set left to check it on.

"Test fewer, with a stricter bar" is better because it cuts the chance of a fluke while you are still planning, and it keeps the holdout set untouched for that one final confirmation.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Run each idea once to save money”?
check:2:2.a:
"Run each idea once to save money" sounds sensible. Saving money is a fair goal, and nothing in the lesson says you must run each idea many times.

But it doesn't touch the real danger. The danger comes from **how many comparisons** you make. A comparison means checking one prompt idea against the baseline, your current version. Each comparison has about a 5% chance of a **false positive**, a "win" that is really just luck.

With 50 ideas, you still make 50 comparisons, whether you run each once or not. The lesson's table shows that 20 comparisons already give about a 64% chance that at least one wins by luck. With 50, that chance is even higher. So you would very likely crown a fluke and think you found a better prompt. Running each idea once leaves the count at 50, so the risk stays just as high.

"Test fewer, with a stricter bar" is better because it attacks the cause directly: it cuts the number of comparisons and divides the 5% by that number (the **Bonferroni** correction), so a lucky win is much harder to get.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Chance of at least one fluke” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

**The problem.** "Each comparison has about a 5% chance of naming a winner by pure luck. That's a false positive. If I test many prompt variants, those small chances add up."

**The idea.** "Each test has a 95% chance of *not* fooling me. For none of them to fool me, every single test has to come out clean, and that gets less likely with every test I add. Flip it around, and the chance of at least one fluke grows fast. With 20 variants, it's about 64%. It's like rolling a die. One roll rarely gives a six, but roll enough times and one turns up."

**A trade-off.** "The Bonferroni fix divides the 5% by the number of tests. That's strict. It blocks flukes, but it can also hide a real, small improvement."

**A likely follow-up**

*"So how would you pick a prompt honestly?"*

Hint: give two guards.
- Limit how many variants you try.
- Confirm the winner **once** on the holdout set. That's the examples it has never seen. In MLflow, that's a single run tagged `split = holdout`.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The winner's score sags later.** It looked great on the dev set (the examples you tuned on). Then it scores lower on the holdout set, or users find it no better than the old version.
- **Lots of variants, small lead.** You tried many prompts and the best one beat the rest by only a point or two. With many tries, a small lead like that is often just luck.
- **The holdout set gets reused.** In MLflow you see several runs tagged `split = holdout` for the same search. Each extra look turns the holdout into another chance for a fluke, so it stops being a fair check.
- **Nobody counted the comparisons.** The report gives one best score but not how many variants were tried. Without that number, you can't judge how much luck is in it.

**Quickest check**

Count the dev runs in the experiment. That is how many variants you compared. Then run the winner on the holdout set once. If its holdout score is clearly below its dev score, the dev result was partly luck. If the two scores are close, the win is more likely real.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where the rule needs extra care.

**Your variants are near-copies.** The 64% figure assumes each comparison is a separate coin flip. Ten prompts that differ by one word tend to win or lose together, so the real fluke risk is lower and Bonferroni (dividing 5% by the count) becomes too strict. Test fewer, more distinct variants, and still confirm the winner once on the holdout.

**You keep checking the holdout.** The holdout only protects you if the winner sees it once. If you peek, tweak, and re-check, it quietly becomes a second dev set, and its score turns optimistic too. When you need another confirmation, set aside a fresh holdout.

**The scores themselves are noisy.** An LLM can answer differently each time, and an LLM judge (a model that grades answers) can wobble too. On a small holdout, that noise can hide a real gain or fake one. Run each example a few times, average the scores, and grow the holdout until results stay steady.

learn:term.a:
They aren't two of the same kind of thing. **Design** is a stage of your work. **Bonferroni** is one tool you can use during that stage.

**Design** is the planning step, before you run any tests. Here you decide what to compare and how many variants to try. The first guard lives here: keep the number small. Fewer comparisons means fewer chances for a lucky win.

**Bonferroni** is a specific rule you can apply while designing. You take the usual 5% threshold (the bar a result must clear to count as a win) and divide it by the number of comparisons. That makes each win harder to get by luck.

How they work together, using the lesson's table:

- Design says: "Try 5 variants, not 20." The fluke chance drops from 64% to 23%.
- Bonferroni then says: "With 5 comparisons, use 1% instead of 5%." That pushes the fluke risk down further.

Everyday comparison: Design is planning a road trip. Bonferroni is one rule in that plan, like "drive slower when the route is longer." The plan comes first, and the rule is something you choose to add to it.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the road-trip analogy is loose but not wrong, and the length is near the limit.

check:0:0.q: Why not “A is better: it won 12 of the 20”?
check:0:0.a:
"A is better: it won 12 of the 20" gets one thing right. It looks only at the 20 disagreements, the examples where one setup passed and the other failed. That is the correct place to look. The 180 examples where both agreed tell you nothing about which is better.

What it misses is whether 12 to 8 is a big enough split to trust. Imagine A and B are truly equal. Each disagreement would then be like a coin flip. Flip a coin 20 times and you will often get 12 heads and 8 tails, just by chance. So a 12 to 8 split is exactly what luck alone tends to produce.

The lesson gives a line to check against. With 20 disagreements, the gap needs to be about 9 or more. Here the gap is 12 minus 8, which is 4. That is well short of 9, so the result is not **statistically significant**, meaning it is not too big to be luck.

"Too close to call on 20 disagreements" is better because it checks the gap against the line McNemar's test sets, instead of just trusting whoever scored higher.

check:0:2.q: Why not “B is better: 8 wins is a fair share”?
check:0:2.a:
This option gets one thing right. B did win 8 of the disagreements, so B is not hopeless. It beats A on some questions.

But it misses the main point in two ways.

First, it picks the wrong side. A won 12 and B won 8. If either setup were ahead, it would be A, not B. Winning "a fair share" just means B kept up. It doesn't make B the better one.

Second, the real question is whether the gap is too big to be luck. The gap here is 12 minus 8, which is 4. For 20 disagreements, the rule of thumb from McNemar's test says the gap needs to be about 9 or more. (McNemar's test is the standard check for pass/fail results on the same examples.) A gap of 4 is well below that line. A split like 12 to 8 could easily come from chance.

Also notice that the 180 questions where A and B agreed tell you nothing. Only the 20 disagreements count.

"Too close to call on 20 disagreements" is better because it checks the gap against the line for that many disagreements and admits that neither setup has clearly won.

check:1:0.a:
"All 100 questions" gets one thing right. You do need to run both setups on every question. That is how you find out where they agree and where they don't.

But it misses the key point. On the 90 questions where both got the same result, the score goes up or down equally for A and B. A question both passed shows they are both capable there. A question both failed shows it is hard for both. Neither one tells you which setup is *better*, because they behaved the same. Mixing those 90 in just hides the real signal behind a lot of ties.

The useful evidence sits only in the 10 disagreements. That means the questions A passed and B failed, plus the ones B passed and A failed. You count each side and look at the gap. Then you check whether that gap is big enough not to be luck, using McNemar's test. That is the standard check for pass/fail results on the same examples.

"The 10 where they disagree" is better because those are the only questions where A and B behaved differently, so only they can show which one is better.

judge.notes: No real problems; it stays close to the lesson, though McNemar's test is named without being explained and the answer is close to the 200-word limit.

check:1:1.a:
It's a natural pick. The 90 are most of the data, and it feels like more data should tell you more.

**What it gets right:** those 90 questions do tell you something. If both setups passed most of them, you know both are fairly strong. If both failed, you've found questions that are hard for everyone. That's useful for judging the eval set or the task.

**What it misses:** the question asks which setup is *better*. On those 90, A and B got the same result. When both pass, neither earns a point over the other. When both fail, neither loses one. So those questions can't separate them, however many there are. Adding them in only blurs the picture.

This is the heart of a **paired comparison** (running both setups on the same examples and comparing them one example at a time). A question that is easy or hard for both cancels out. You're left with the cases where they truly differ.

**Why "The 10 where they disagree" is right:** only on those 10 did one setup pass where the other failed, so only they show which one is better.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Run each one more time”?
check:2:1.a:
Running each setup again does have one thing going for it. Models can give slightly different answers from run to run, so a second run shows how much of the score is just that kind of wobble.

But it doesn't fix the real problem. A and B would still be answering **different questions**. If A's set happened to be easier, A looks better no matter how many times you rerun it. More runs on mismatched sets give you more numbers, but not a fairer comparison.

A paired comparison needs every question to have two results, one from A and one from B. Only then can you line them up row by row and spot the **disagreements**, the questions where one passed and the other failed. With separate question sets there are no matching rows. There is nothing to pair.

Running both on the same questions is better because each question's difficulty hits A and B equally and cancels out, so the disagreements show the true difference between them.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Use a bigger judge model”?
check:2:2.a:
A bigger judge model doesn't fix what's missing. A "judge model" is the AI that grades each answer as pass or fail. A bigger one might grade more accurately. That part is a fair instinct: sloppy grading adds noise to any comparison.

But the problem here isn't the grading. A and B each ran on their own set of questions. A paired comparison works by lining up the two results for the same question and asking "did they agree or disagree?" With different questions, there are no pairs to line up. Question 7 for A and question 7 for B are different questions, so comparing them tells you nothing.

That's also why pairing is so sensitive. A hard question is hard for both setups, so its difficulty cancels out. With separate question sets, one setup might simply have gotten easier questions. No judge, however big, can undo that.

So even perfect grading leaves you comparing two overall scores, not counting disagreements.

"Run both on the same questions" is better because it creates the matched pairs that a paired comparison, and McNemar's test, needs in the first place.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Count only the disagreements” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem.* "Prompt A scores 72% on our eval set and prompt B scores 68%. Is A really better, or did it just get lucky?"

*The idea.* "I run both on the same examples and compare them one example at a time. If both pass, or both fail, that example tells me nothing about which is better. Only the disagreements count: A passed where B failed, or the reverse. If those split roughly evenly, the difference is luck. McNemar's test, the standard check for pass/fail results, says how lopsided the split must be. With 20 disagreements, the gap needs to be about 9."

*The edge case.* "With fewer than about 25 disagreements, the quick rule is too generous. A 5-to-0 split passes it, but the exact version of the test says it could still be luck. So I'd gather more examples before declaring a winner."

**Likely follow-up**

"Why not just compare the two overall scores?"

*Hint for a strong answer:* A hard example is hard for both setups. Pairing cancels out that shared difficulty. Two separate overall scores keep it in as noise, so they can hide a real difference.

judge.notes: No real problems; it is about 195 words, just under the limit, and 'gap' is used without a one-line definition, which is a minor weakness.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **A winner picked from two totals.** Someone says "A got 82%, B got 79%, A wins" without counting the disagreements. In real use the two setups then look about the same.
- **The examples did not match.** A and B ran on different test questions, or the results were saved in a different order. Then row q2 for A is not the same question as row q2 for B, and every comparison is mixed up.
- **Agreements were counted.** If the "disagreement" numbers add up to nearly the whole test set, the questions where both passed or both failed were wrongly included.
- **A tiny gap was called a win.** For example, 12 to 8 on 20 disagreements was reported as a clear victory.
- **Only totals in MLflow.** The run logs a single score but no `a_only` and `b_only` counts, so nobody can recheck the result.

**Quickest check**

Put the two result sheets side by side. Confirm that each row shows the same question for both setups. Count the rows where only A passed and the rows where only B passed. Then compare the gap to the line: about 9 for 20 disagreements, 20 for 100, and 40 for 400.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where this rule needs extra care.

**1. Very few disagreements.** Below about 25 disagreements, the "gap times itself versus 4 times the disagreements" shortcut is too generous, so a lopsided split like 5 to 0 can slip through. Use the exact version of McNemar's test, which counts every possible split, or add more examples so you get more disagreements.

**2. An LLM app whose answers vary.** An LLM (large language model) can pass an example on one run and fail it on the next, so some disagreements are just random wobble, not real differences between A and B. Run each example a few times and use the majority result. Where you can, also set temperature, the setting that controls how random the output is, to zero.

**3. Comparing many setups at once.** Every extra comparison is another chance for luck to look like a real win. Ask for a bigger gap than usual, or pick your finalists on one eval set and confirm the winner on fresh examples.

learn:term.a:
**Paired comparison** means you test both setups on the exact same examples and compare them one example at a time.

**An everyday version:** Two friends take the same quiz. You could just compare their final scores. But it's fairer to go question by question. If a question was very hard, it was hard for both of them. That tells you nothing about who is better. What matters is the questions where one got it right and the other got it wrong.

**In the lesson's example:** Each row in the table is one "pair", meaning A's result and B's result on the same example.

- `q1`: both passed. They agree, so ignore it.
- `q4`: both failed. They agree, so ignore it.
- `q2`: only A passed. That's a point for A.
- `q3`: only B passed. That's a point for B.

You keep only the disagreements and count them. With 20 disagreements, a 15 to 5 split is a gap of 10. That clears the line of about 9, so A really wins. A 12 to 8 split is a gap of 4, which is too close to call.

Pairing makes the comparison sharper. Difficulty that both setups share simply cancels out.

check:0:0.a:
"12" comes from adding: 4 chunk sizes + 5 values of k + 3 models. That does get one thing right. It counts every value you want to try, and none are missed.

But adding only works if you change one setting at a time and leave the others alone. A full grid search tries every combination. Each chunk size is paired with every value of k. Each of those pairs is then tried with every model.

Build it up step by step:

- 4 chunk sizes, each with 5 values of k, gives 4 × 5 = 20 pairs.
- Each of those 20 pairs runs with 3 models, which gives 20 × 3 = 60 runs.

It's the getting-dressed idea from the lesson. 2 shirts and 3 trousers give 6 outfits, not 5. Each new setting multiplies the count. It doesn't add to it.

This matters for cost. Every run pays for its own eval and judge calls. So 60 runs costs five times what 12 would.

"60" is better because a full grid multiplies the number of values in each setting (4 × 5 × 3), so every possible combination gets its own run.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The arithmetic (4×5×3=60, five times 12) and the shirts-and-trousers example match the lesson. The aside about changing one setting at a time goes slightly beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

check:0:2.a:
"20" is a good start. It comes from 4 chunk sizes times 5 values of `k`. That is the right move: you multiply, you don't add. Every chunk size gets paired with every `k`, so you get 20 pairs.

What it misses is the third setting, the models. A full grid means every combination of every setting you planned to vary. Each of those 20 pairs still has to be tried with each of the 3 models. So each pair turns into 3 runs.

Think of the getting-dressed picture. 4 shirts and 5 trousers give 20 outfits. Then you add 3 hats. Each outfit can go with any hat, so you have 20 times 3 outfits. You don't stop at 20 just because the hats came last.

This is why the lesson says to count before you start. Forgetting one setting makes the plan look three times cheaper than it is. Each run pays for eval and judge calls, so that gap is real money.

"60" is better because it multiplies all three settings, 4 × 5 × 3, so it counts every run the grid will actually make.

check:1:0.q: Why not “It goes up by just one run”?
check:1:0.a:
"It goes up by just one run" gets one thing right. You are adding exactly one new value: a single extra model in the model list.

What it misses is how a grid works. A grid search tries every combination of values. So the new model does not get one run. It gets paired with every chunk size and every value of `k`, just like the other two models.

Here is a small example. Say you have 2 chunk sizes and 2 values of `k`. That makes 4 combinations for each model.

- 2 models: 4 times 2 is 8 runs.
- 3 models: 4 times 3 is 12 runs.

Adding one model added 4 runs, not 1. Each of those runs pays for its own eval and judge calls, so the cost grows by the same amount. Think of the outfits idea: adding one more shirt gives you a new outfit for every pair of trousers you own, not just one.

"Every chunk size and k runs again for it" is better because it shows that one new value multiplies the runs instead of adding a single run.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Nothing until the next grid”?
check:1:2.a:
"Nothing until the next grid" gets one small thing right. Runs you have already finished don't change. Their results stay logged in MLflow, untouched.

But it treats the new model as something separate, to be dealt with later. That's not how a grid works. A grid is every combination of the values you listed. The moment the third model joins the list of models, it becomes part of the grid. It has to be paired with every chunk size and every value of `k`, just like the first two models were.

So the number of runs doesn't stay the same. It grows by a whole extra block. If you had 2 chunk sizes and 2 values of `k`, that's 4 combinations per model. Two models meant 8 runs. Three models means 12. Each new run also pays for its own eval and judge calls, so the cost grows by the same amount.

"Every chunk size and k runs again for it" is better because it names exactly what adding a value does: the new model repeats the full set of other combinations, so the run count multiplies instead of staying flat.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The only small point is the claim that finished runs stay logged in MLflow, which the lesson doesn't state outright, though it fits the lesson's MLflow setup.

check:2:0.a:
"Which model will win" is a fair thing to care about. It is the reason you run the experiment in the first place. So the instinct is good.

The problem is timing. You cannot work out the winner *before* you start. That answer only comes from the runs themselves. If you could guess it ahead of time, you would not need the experiment.

What you *can* work out beforehand is the size of the job. Every value you add multiplies the number of runs:

- 5 chunk sizes
- times 4 values of `k` (how many pieces to fetch for each question)
- times 2 models

That is 40 runs. Each run pays for its eval calls and its judge calls. The judge is the model that scores the answers. Forty runs could cost far more time and money than you expected. You might decide to trim the grid first, perhaps by trying fewer chunk sizes.

"How many runs, and what they cost" is the better answer. It is something you can actually calculate before starting, and it tells you whether the plan is worth running at all.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Which chunk size is best”?
check:2:1.a:
"Which chunk size is best" is a fair thing to care about. It is often the reason you run the experiment in the first place. So the instinct is right.

The problem is timing. You can't know which chunk size is best before you start. That is the answer the runs will give you. It is the result, not part of the plan.

The question asks what to work out *before* you start. The thing you can work out up front is the size of the job. Every value you add multiplies the number of runs:

- 5 chunk sizes
- times 4 values of `k` (how many pieces to fetch per question)
- times 2 models
- equals 40 runs

Each of those 40 runs pays for eval calls and judge calls. A judge is the model that scores the answers. That adds up fast. If 40 runs is too slow or too expensive, you want to know now, so you can trim the grid. For example, you might test 3 chunk sizes instead of 5.

"How many runs, and what they cost" is better because it is the one thing you can calculate before spending anything, and it tells you whether the plan is worth running.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Grow combinations setting by setting” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

**The problem:** "I want to try every mix of a few settings, like chunk size, `k`, and model. Writing out every mix by hand is slow and easy to get wrong."

**The idea:** "So I build the list one setting at a time. I start with one empty mix. For each new setting, I take every mix I have so far and make one copy per value, adding that value. It's like getting dressed. 2 shirts and 3 trousers give 6 outfits. Add 2 hats and you get 12. Each setting multiplies the count."

**The trade-off:** "That multiplying is the catch. Every run pays for eval and judge calls, so I count the runs and the cost before starting. One small detail: I make real copies of each mix. Otherwise, changing one mix would quietly change the others too."

**A likely follow-up**

*"What if the grid is too big to afford?"*

Hint: Say you would cut it down first. You could fix settings you already trust. You could try a few values widely spaced, then zoom in near the best one. Or you could pick a random sample of mixes instead of all of them. This is called a **random search**.
